Issue 1 - September 2026

1. Purpose and scope

The purpose of this policy is to affirm that all workers have the right to work in an environment where they are treated with dignity, respect and fairness. Any form of harassment, sexual harassment, bullying, discrimination or victimisation are unacceptable forms of behaviour at UKAEA and will not be permitted, condoned, or tolerated under any circumstances.

If any individual is found to have committed, authorised, or condoned an act of bullying, harassment or discrimination, UKAEA will take appropriate and proportionate action in accordance with our Disciplinary Procedure. This may include, where applicable, disciplinary measures up to and including summary dismissal. In the case of contractors or third parties, such behaviour may result in termination of engagement or other appropriate contractual remedies.

This policy applies to all individuals working for or engaged by UKAEA, including employees, contractors, agency workers, consultants, and apprentices. It also applies to job applicants and is relevant at every stage of the employment lifecycle.

The policy extends to all workplace interactions and environments, whether taking place on UKAEA premises, at off-site locations, or in virtual or hybrid working settings. It also applies to work-related social activities, training events, conferences, and business travel.

This policy extends to the use of social media and other online platforms where individuals are identifiable as being associated with UKAEA, or where the content visible has a clear connection to their role or activities within the organisation.

In addition, the policy covers instances of harassment, sexual harassment, bullying, discrimination, victimisation or other forms of inappropriate behaviour carried out by third parties, such as customers, suppliers, visitors, or other stakeholders with whom UKAEA workers may come into contact in the course of their work.

2. Definitions

2.1 Harassment

Harassment is defined as unwanted behaviour related to a protected characteristic and is unlawful. Harassment, under the Equality Act 2010, has the purpose or effect of:

violating someone else’s dignity

creating an intimidating, hostile, degrading, humiliating or offensive environment for someone else

Harassment can also occur in the following circumstances:

perception - where a person is subjected to harassment because they are perceived to have a protected characteristic, even if that perception is incorrect

association – where a person is harassed because of their association with someone who has a protected characteristic

The key factor is how the behaviour is experienced by the recipient. Conduct that may seem trivial or harmless to one person may have a profound impact on another. All workers are therefore expected to exercise sensitivity, professionalism, and respect in their interactions.

Under the Equality Act 2010, there are nine protected characteristics. These are:

age

disability

gender reassignment

marriage or civil partnership

pregnancy and maternity

race

sexual orientation

religion or belief

sex

2.2 Examples of harassment

Harassment can take many forms. It may be verbal, non-verbal, written, physical, or online, and can occur in person, via email, telephone, messaging platforms, or social media. Examples include (but are not limited to):

Verbal

Offensive jokes, comments, or ‘banter’ about someone’s protected characteristic; derogatory terms or name-calling; mocking accents, appearance, or abilities; unwelcome remarks about a person’s body, dress, or private life.

Non-verbal

Displaying offensive images, posters, or gestures that target a protected characteristic; using facial expressions or body language to demean someone because of a protected characteristic.

Physical

Unwanted touching, pushing, or other physical contact connected to a protected characteristic; intimidating body language or gestures; invading personal space in a way that targets someone’s protected characteristic.

Written or digital

Sending offensive emails, texts, or social media messages related to a protected characteristic; circulating inappropriate images, memes, or rumours about a colleague because of a protected characteristic; deliberately excluding someone from work-related communications or groups due to a protected characteristic.

Sexual

Sexual harassment is unwanted behaviour of a sexual nature, and does not need to be related to a protected characteristic. More information can be found in the following section.

Harassment by perception or association

Teasing, isolating, or discriminating against someone because they are perceived to have a protected characteristic, even if inaccurate; harassing an individual because of their association with someone who has a protected characteristic (for example: family member, partner, or friend).

2.3 Sexual harassment

Sexual harassment is a form of harassment that is sexual in nature. Sexual harassment is unlawful and under the Equality Act 2010, it is defined as:

conduct of a sexual nature that has the purpose or effect of:

violating an individual’s dignity

creating an intimidating, hostile, degrading, humiliating, or offensive environment

less favourable treatment related to sex or gender reassignment that occurs because of a rejection of, or submission to, sexual conduct

2.4 Examples of sexual harassment

Sexual harassment can take many forms and may occur at work, outside work, in person, or online. It may involve a single incident or a series of incidents. Importantly, sexual harassment is determined by how the behaviour is perceived by the recipient, not by the intent of the person engaging in the conduct, and can affect any individual regardless of their position, gender, or relationship to the perpetrator. Examples include (but are not limited to):

Verbal

Persistent suggestions to meet socially after refusal; unwelcome sexual advances or propositions; intrusive questions about a person’s sex or gender; suggestive remarks; gender-related insults; offensive comments about appearance or dress; innuendo or lewd comments; explicit discussion of own sex life.

Physical

Unwanted touching, hugging, kissing, or patting; invading personal space or blocking someone intimidatingly; sexual assault or coercive physical behaviour.

Non-verbal

Leering, whistling, sexually suggestive gestures; displaying offensive, pornographic, or inappropriate material.

Written or digital

Sending offensive, pornographic, or sexually suggestive material via text, email, video, social media, communication platforms or shared documents; posting inappropriate content online about a colleague.

Gossip or speculation

Spreading rumours or making derogatory comments about a person’s sexual orientation, gender identity, or alleged sexual behaviour.

Quid pro quo

Offering promotions, pay raises, or benefits in exchange for sexual favours; threatening demotion or negative treatment if sexual demands are refused.

Retaliation / Victimisation

Any adverse action taken against someone for reporting harassment or supporting a complainant.

2.5 Bullying

There is no legal definition of bullying. However, for the purposes of this policy, bullying is regarded as behaviour that is offensive, intimidating, malicious, insulting, or an abuse or misuse of power. It is often persistent, and has the effect, whether intended or perceived, of undermining, humiliating, or causing harm, emotionally or psychologically, to the recipient.

2.6 Examples of bullying

Bullying can take many forms, including physical, verbal, or non-verbal conduct. It is not limited to face-to-face interactions and may occur through email, phone calls, instant messaging, online platforms, or social media. While bullying may occur in the workplace, it can also take place outside of work, including during work-related activities, business travel, training events, or social functions connected to employment.

Bullying can affect anyone, regardless of their role or level within the organisation, and can be directed towards individuals or groups. Examples include (but are not limited to):

Verbal

Shouting, swearing, or aggressive language; persistent criticism; name-calling or belittling.

Physical

Pushing, hitting, or any form of physical intimidation; damaging someone’s property.

Psychological / Emotional

Ignoring or excluding someone; isolating them from work or social activities; setting unrealistic deadlines or workload to cause stress; undermining or deliberately sabotaging work.

Digital / Online

Sending threatening or abusive emails, texts, or messages; sharing humiliating content about someone online; cyberbullying on social media or messaging platforms.

Gossip or speculation

Spreading malicious rumours about someone’s personal life, work performance, or behaviour; making false or misleading statements intended to damage reputation; circulating private information without consent.

Abuse of power

Using authority to intimidate, control, or manipulate someone; blocking opportunities for promotion or training unfairly.

2.7 Discrimination

Discrimination occurs when an individual is treated unfairly or less favourably because of a protected characteristic, as defined under the Equality Act 2010 and listed under the harassment section of this policy. Discrimination can arise in many aspects of the workplace, including recruitment, training, promotion, performance management, dismissal, and day-to-day working relationships.

2.8 Examples of discrimination

There are several forms of discrimination under the Equality Act 2010:

Direct discrimination

Treating someone less favourably because of a protected characteristic.

Indirect discrimination

Applying a policy, practice, or rule that appears neutral but disproportionately disadvantages people with a protected characteristic, unless it can be objectively justified.

Discrimination arising from disability

Treating a disabled person unfavourably because of something connected with their disability, where such treatment cannot be justified.

Failure to make reasonable adjustments

Not making appropriate changes to remove barriers that place a disabled person at a substantial disadvantage compared to others.

By perception

Discriminating against someone because they are perceived to have a protected characteristic, even if that perception is incorrect.

By association

Discriminating against someone because of their association with a person who has a protected characteristic (e.g., a family member or partner).

2.9 Victimisation

Victimisation is defined under the Equality Act 2010 as treating someone unfairly or subjecting them to a detriment because they have:

made, or intend to make, a complaint or allegation of discrimination, harassment, or bullying

supported another person in making such a complaint (for example, by giving evidence or acting as a witness)

raised concerns about breaches of equality, diversity, or inclusion

Victimisation is unlawful, regardless of whether the original complaint is upheld, provided it was made in good faith.

The key factor is that victimisation occurs as a reaction to an individual exercising their rights under equality law. It can take many forms and may be overt or subtle. All workers are expected to treat colleagues who raise concerns with respect and professionalism, and to ensure they are not disadvantaged for doing so.

2.10 Examples of victimisation

Victimisation can occur in different ways and may be verbal, non-verbal, written, physical, or digital. Examples include (but are not limited to):

Verbal

Making negative remarks about a colleague for raising a grievance; pressuring someone to withdraw a complaint; spreading rumours about a person who has supported another’s complaint.

Non-verbal

Excluding someone from meetings or workplace activities because they gave evidence in a discrimination case; deliberately ignoring or ostracising a colleague.

Physical

Withdrawing work opportunities, training, or resources from someone because they raised concerns about discrimination or harassment.

Written or digital

Sending hostile or dismissive emails to someone who submitted a complaint; leaving them out of work-related communication channels.

Workplace treatment

Denying promotion, giving unfair performance reviews, changing duties, or threatening dismissal because an employee made or supported a complaint under the Equality Act.

3. References

Equality Act 2010.

4. Responsibilities

Role Responsibilities

Workers / Employees All workers are expected to take personal responsibility for observing, upholding, promoting, and applying this policy. Workers are advised to be mindful of their behaviour at all times and consider how this may be perceived by others. Workers are strongly encouraged to report any experiences of any form harassment, sexual harassment, bullying, discrimination or victimisation.

Managers, Line Managers and Investigating Manager Effectively implement this policy in support of employees

Head of Employee Relations Ensure Trade Union consultation is undertaken when considering changes or updates to this document.

Document Author Ensure the document is reviewed every year.

5. Data protection

We will process any personal data collected in accordance with our data protection policy. In particular, we will record only the personal information required and keep the information only for as long as necessary.

6. Monitoring and review

This policy is reviewed annually and, if necessary, amended to ensure that it remains effective. We analyse data around allegations of bullying or harassment (in compliance with our data protection obligations) on an ongoing basis to assess the impact of this policy and our wider equality, diversity, and inclusion strategy.

7. Our commitment

UKAEA is a diverse and international organisation that values and celebrates differences. We are committed to fostering an inclusive environment where diversity is respected, supported, and never used as a basis for exclusion. Central to this commitment is our Dignity at Work approach, which ensures that all individuals are treated with fairness, courtesy, and respect, enabling everyone to contribute and thrive in a positive working environment. As part of our commitment we will take all reasonable steps to prevent harassment, bullying and victimisation by:

ensuring all new starters have access to equality, diversity and inclusion related training and anti-bullying and anti-harassment training, as part of their onboarding programme

ensuring all employees have the opportunity to attend regular equality, diversity and inclusion related training and anti-bullying and anti-harassment training on at least an annual basis

providing additional training for line managers to ensure that they understand how to implement this policy effectively and their role in preventing and stopping bullying and harassment from occurring in the workplace and by third parties that you may have contact with

monitoring our workplace culture through anonymous surveys, exit interviews, one-to-one conversations, return-to-work meetings and employee networks to identify and address any issues

undertaking regular risk assessments to determine all reasonable measures that can be implemented to minimise the risk of exposure to sexual harassment in the workplace and by third parties that you may have contact with

ensuring that our zero-tolerance approach to all forms of discrimination, and bullying and harassment, is communicated to all workers and third parties that you may have contact with

UKAEA will provide learning and development to ensure all staff have access to relevant personal development to enable everyone to understand issues linked to diversity and work effectively in diverse groups. Staff are expected to take opportunities to educate themselves and managers are expected to allow sufficient time to enable this development.

7.1 Our commitment – third parties

Third party harassment occurs when an employee is subjected to harassment by someone who is not employed by UKAEA but who UKAEA workers may come into contact within in the course of their work, for example customers, suppliers or visitors. Any form of third-party harassment, sexual harassment, bullying, discrimination or victimisation will not be permitted, condoned, or tolerated under any circumstances.

By law, UKAEA is required to take all reasonable steps to prevent harassment and sexual harassment by third parties. In order to prevent third party harassment, bullying, discrimination and victimisation from taking place, we will:

require all new and existing suppliers to sign the UKAEA Supplier Commitment to Comply with Behaviour and Reporting Requirements, confirming their commitment to uphold UKAEA’s zero-tolerance approach to actual or suspected harassment, bullying, victimisation and unlawful discrimination

ensure this policy is available to third parties through our company website

encourage employees to report any actual or suspected third-party harassment, bullying, discrimination or victimisation through the reporting channels available to them, including anonymous reporting, their line manager, or the People and Culture Team

8. Expectations and responsibilities

All workers are expected to take personal responsibility for observing, upholding, promoting, and applying this policy. Regardless of position or seniority, every individual has a duty to contribute to a respectful, inclusive, and safe working environment. Commitment to these principles is an integral part of everyone’s role within UKAEA and is essential to fostering a positive and collaborative workplace culture.

Any dealings workers have with third parties, including customers, suppliers, contractors, agency staff and consultants, must be free from harassment, sexual harassment, bullying, discrimination or victimisation.

All workers are advised to be mindful of their behaviour at all times and consider how this may be perceived by others. Conduct may constitute as harassment regardless of the individual’s intention or motive. What one person may consider a ‘joke’ can be offensive to another. Furthermore, a single action can amount to harassment if it is sufficiently serious.

All workers may be held personally liable for acts of discrimination and/or harassment. Personal liability means that individuals can be held legally and disciplinarily responsible for their behaviour, regardless of whether it was committed intentionally or negligently. This includes conduct that violates this policy, or applicable laws related to discrimination, harassment, bullying or victimisation.

If any individual experiences or witnesses any form harassment, sexual harassment, bullying, discrimination or victimisation they are strongly encouraged to report it promptly to their line manager or a member of the People and Culture team. Early reporting helps ensure that appropriate support and action can be taken in a timely manner.

8.1 How complaints and allegations will be managed

Complaints and allegations of harassment, sexual harassment, bullying, discrimination, or victimisation may be raised in several ways: informally, formally, or anonymously. Further guidance on how to raise a concern can be found in the supporting documents.

All allegations raised through the formal procedure will be investigated thoroughly and addressed under the relevant Grievance Policy and / or Disciplinary Policy and Procedure. Where behaviour is found to constitute gross misconduct, this may result in disciplinary action up to and including summary dismissal (dismissal without notice).

The UKAEA is committed to handling all complaints and allegations in an impartial, fair, and timely manner. In doing so, we will:

ensure all formal complaints are investigated promptly, thoroughly, and impartially

protect the dignity, rights, and wellbeing of all parties involved, including complainants, respondents, and witnesses, ensuring that no individual is subject to unfair treatment or retaliation

ensure that investigating managers act with the highest standards of professionalism, fairness, and discretion. All concerns will be listened to respectfully, without bias, judgement, or minimisation

adopt a compassionate, people-centred approach and provide appropriate support to those involved, including access to employee support services where required

ensure that investigations and outcomes are progressed without unnecessary delay, balancing the need for thoroughness with the importance of timely resolution

ensure investigations and outcomes take into account any aggravating factors, such as an abuse of power or authority over a more junior colleague

8.2 How third-party complaints and allegations will be managed

Where the alleged bully or harasser is a third party (for example, a contractor, client, or visitor), the procedure outlined in this policy may need to be adapted to reflect the circumstances. In such cases, UKAEA will take reasonable steps to ensure that a fair and thorough investigation is conducted, liaising with the relevant third party or their employer where appropriate to address the matter. If any allegation of harassment by a third-party proves to be well-founded, steps taken by UKAEA may include warning the individual about the inappropriate nature of their behaviour, banning the individual from UKAEA premises, reporting individual actions to the individual’s employer and/or relevant authorities including the police.

8.3 Support for those affected or involved

It is recognised that anyone affected by, or involved in, a complaint of bullying or harassment may feel anxious, distressed, or uncertain about what will happen next. UKAEA are committed to providing appropriate support and ensuring that everyone involved is treated with empathy and respect throughout the process.

If an employee feels unable to continue working in close contact with the alleged bully or harasser, UKAEA will give careful and compassionate consideration to any requests for temporary adjustments to working arrangements while the matter is under investigation.

Employees can access free, confidential emotional support through the Employee Assistance Programme (EAP). Details can be found on Nucleus. In addition, employees may wish to seek support from a member of the People and Culture Team, internal staff networks or our team of Mental Health First Aiders, who will be able to signpost to further support. Members of our recognised trade union can also contact their union representative for advice and support throughout the process.

Non-UKAEA employees who are affected by or involved in a complaint are encouraged to contact their own employer for access to support services or resources available to them.

Anyone who raises a complaint or participates in good faith in a bullying or harassment investigation must not experience any form of detrimental treatment or victimisation. If an employee believes they have been treated unfairly as a result of raising or participating in such a matter, they should inform their line manager or the People and Culture team as soon as possible.

Regardless of the outcome of a complaint, UKAEA will carefully consider how best to manage any ongoing working relationship between the individuals involved, including any third parties. This may include, where appropriate, adjustments to job duties, work location, or reporting lines, or the offer of workplace mediation to help rebuild a positive and respectful working environment.

Employees who require time away from work relating to a complaint of bullying, harassment or sexual harassment should discuss this with their line manager or, where the concern involves their line manager, an alternative manager or the People & Culture Team. Requests for annual leave or sickness absence will be managed in line with the Absences & Leave Policy and Sickness Absence Policy, as appropriate.

8.4 Sensitivity and confidentiality

Confidentiality, and trust in that confidentiality, is essential when handling allegations of inappropriate behaviour. All individuals involved in an informal or formal complaint process concerning harassment, sexual harassment, bullying, discrimination, or victimisation, including complainants, respondents, witnesses, and those supporting the process, are required to maintain strict confidentiality at all times.

Information relating to a complaint, including the identities of the individuals concerned, must only be shared on a genuine “need-to-know” basis and only with those who are formally involved in managing or investigating the matter. This requirement is in place to protect the integrity of the process, uphold fairness, and safeguard the dignity and wellbeing of all parties.

Breaches of confidentiality, or behaviour that demonstrates a lack of sensitivity, professionalism, or respect for the process, will be treated seriously. For employees, this may result in disciplinary action, up to and including dismissal. For non-employees (such as contractors, agency workers, or visitors), other appropriate action may be taken, which could include termination of engagement or removal of access to the workplace.

8.5 Malicious or vexatious complaints

A malicious complaint is one that is made with the intention to intimidate, to lower the reputation of, or otherwise injure or harm somebody, through knowingly providing false or misleading information or withholding information about an incident or issue.

A vexatious complaint is either one that is made with the sole or main intention to harass, annoy or subdue somebody, or one that is unreasonable, without foundation, frivolous, repetitive, deliberately burdensome or unwarranted.

Making a malicious or vexatious complaint is regarded as misconduct and may result in disciplinary action, up to and including summary dismissal.

UKAEA recognises the importance of distinguishing between a complaint that is not upheld (because evidence does not support it) and a complaint that is deliberately false or malicious. Employees will not be penalised for raising a concern in good faith, even if it cannot be substantiated.
